pub: New York State Law Reporting Bureau
author: Supreme Court of New York, Appellate Division, Second Department (Leventhal, Roman, Cohen & Miller, JJ.)

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source addresses pleading standards for damages and causation in legal-malpractice claims arising from divorce representation. It does not discuss legal AI, task-level capability, verification, selective deployment, or operating-model redesign, so its position on the cluster proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Legal malpractice: Error alone cannot establish liability
st.an: Katsoris directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that legal malpractice requires objectively deficient professional care, proximate causation, and actual, ascertainable damages—not merely an alleged error, settlement, or adverse financial consequence. It also supports the cluster’s treatment of reasonable professional choices, conclusory corrective-fee allegations, and duplicative fiduciary-duty claims.

mo.t: Delegated error: Client relief need not excuse counsel
Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
Lawyer accountability: Discipline and liability remain separate
Market reform: Information and incentives shape access

kp.k: Malpractice requires professional breach and actual, ascertainable damages
kp.d: The court states, quoting Dempster v Liotti, that legal malpractice requires allegations of deficient professional skill and knowledge and actual, ascertainable damages proximately caused by that breach. This September 23, 2020 opinion addresses attorney liability, not AI or changes in legal-service delivery.
qs: To state a cause of action to recover damages for legal malpractice, a plaintiff must allege: (1) that the attorney failed to exercise the ordinary reasonable skill and knowledge commonly possessed by a member of the legal profession; and (2) that the attorney's breach of the duty proximately caused the plaintiff actual and ascertainable damages

kp.k: Reasonable strategic choices do not constitute malpractice
kp.d: The court identifies failures involving procedural rules, conditions precedent, prosecution or defense, and adequate legal research as potential grounds for liability. It distinguishes those failures from selecting among reasonable courses of action, which the Court of Appeals has held does not constitute malpractice.
qs: or for failure to conduct adequate legal research
However, the Court of Appeals has recognized, as a matter of law, that "[the] selection of one among several reasonable courses of action does not constitute malpractice"

kp.k: Causation requires a better outcome absent attorney negligence
kp.d: Quoting Rudolf v Shayne, Dachs, Stanisci, Corker & Sauer, the court states the but-for causation requirement: the plaintiff must show that absent the lawyer’s negligence, the plaintiff would have prevailed in the underlying action or avoided damages.
qs: a plaintiff must show that he or she would have prevailed in the underlying action or would not have incurred any damages, but for the lawyer's negligence

kp.k: Settlement does not automatically preclude a malpractice claim
kp.d: The court explains, quoting Bernstein v Oppenheim & Co., that a malpractice claim can survive settlement if counsel’s mistakes effectively compelled it. Here, the plaintiff’s unsupported assertions of a better trial or settlement outcome did not adequately allege compulsion or establish that declining settlement would have produced a more favorable result.
qs: A claim for legal malpractice is viable, despite settlement of the underlying action, if it is alleged that settlement of the action was effectively compelled by the mistakes of counsel
Moreover, the plaintiff failed to plead specific factual allegations showing that, had he not settled, he would have obtained a more favorable outcome

kp.k: General allegations of financial harm were insufficient
kp.d: The court held that the complaint inadequately alleged actual, ascertainable damages. General references to additional legal fees and financial losses were conclusory; the decision concerns the sufficiency of allegations rather than a factual finding that no losses occurred.
qs: Here, the complaint failed to adequately allege actual, ascertainable damages.

The general allegations that, as a result of the alleged acts of malpractice, the plaintiff was caused to incur "additional legal fees," and caused to suffer "financial damages and expense," "adverse financial consequences," and "direct financial damage," were all conclusory and inadequate to constitute "actual, ascertainable damages"

kp.k: Duplicative fiduciary-duty claims cannot supply a separate recovery theory
kp.d: The court upheld dismissal of the fiduciary-duty cause of action because it arose from the same operative facts as the malpractice claim and alleged no different and distinct damages.
qs: The second cause of action was duplicative of the legal malpractice cause of action, as it arose from the same operative facts, and did not allege different and distinct damages
